arguments.title: Opening Mishnah: Time for evening Shema

issue.summary: Establishes the first Mishnah’s dispute over the end time for evening Shema and Rabban Gamliel’s practical ruling.
issue.details: The Mishnah presents three endpoints for evening Shema: Rabbi Eliezer until the first watch, the Rabbis until midnight, and Rabban Gamliel until dawn. Rabban Gamliel's practical ruling is that his sons may still recite Shema before dawn even after missing the Rabbis' midnight safeguard.

question.summary: Opening Mishnah: Time for evening Shema
question.details: Until what point in the night may one fulfill evening Shema, and how do the opinions in the Mishnah function practically?

position.details: Rabbi Eliezer limits evening Shema to the end of the first watch, treating the early part of the night as the valid period.

reasoning.summary: The first watch defines the night obligation narrowly.
reasoning.details: This reasoning treats the Torah's 'when you lie down' as referring especially to the beginning of the nighttime lying-down period.

underlying_principle.summary: Mitzvah time can be defined by ordinary human behavior.
underlying_principle.details: The time for Shema is tied to the social pattern of going to sleep, so its endpoint can be limited by a recognizable stage of night.

position.details: The Rabbis set midnight as the deadline, functioning as a safeguard against delay even if the biblical time may extend longer.

reasoning.summary: Midnight prevents negligent delay.
reasoning.details: A person who assumes the whole night is available may fall asleep or postpone the mitzvah until it is lost.

underlying_principle.summary: Rabbinic safeguards protect Torah observance.
underlying_principle.details: The Sages may narrow the practical window of a mitzvah to reduce the chance that people will fail to fulfill it.

position.details: Rabban Gamliel rules that one who missed the earlier cutoff may still recite evening Shema until dawn, as he tells his sons after they return late from a wedding.

reasoning.summary: The true nighttime period continues until dawn.
reasoning.details: Since people may still be in the lying-down period until dawn, the underlying obligation has not expired before then.

underlying_principle.summary: Essential validity can exceed a rabbinic safeguard.
underlying_principle.details: A protective deadline shapes ideal practice, but a person who missed it may still rely on the broader mitzvah window.

position.details: Rabban Gamliel's view indicates that the essential time for evening Shema continues as long as people are still in the nighttime period of lying down.

reasoning.summary: The night remains the time of lying down.
reasoning.details: The Torah's category is not exhausted at midnight, so the mitzvah remains valid until dawn.

underlying_principle.summary: Biblical mitzvah time may be broad.
underlying_principle.details: The Torah-defined time can extend beyond the stricter practical deadline used by the Sages.

position.summary: The Rabbis restrict until midnight as a fence

reasoning.summary: People are likely to delay at night.

underlying_principle.summary: A rabbinic fence can narrow practical observance.
underlying_principle.details: The Sages can establish an earlier deadline to protect fulfillment of the mitzvah.
